lead: Every transient so far has been a differential equation with an initial condition bolted on. The Laplace transform removes both difficulties at once: it turns derivatives into multiplication by s, and it swallows the initial condition into the transformed circuit as an extra source. What is left is a network of impedances in the complex variable s, solved with the nodal and mesh tools of Unit 2. The inverse transform at the end returns the time answer. Switched-mode power supplies, motor drives and every SPICE run use this step.
prereq: You need: Chapter 5.1 for i_L(0⁻) and v_C(0⁻), and Chapter 5.3 for the time-domain answers you will check against.

sections.h3: The one-sided transform and the derivative rule

blocks.text: The Laplace transform converts a time function f(t) into a function of the complex variable s = σ + jω: F(s) = ∫₀⁻^∞ f(t) e^(−st) dt. The lower limit is 0⁻, the instant just before switching, so a jump at t = 0 lies inside the integral. That single choice is why initial conditions survive as ordinary numbers instead of constants of integration.

Differentiation becomes multiplication. Apply the rule twice to the RLC loop equation and a second-order differential equation collapses into a quadratic in s — the same characteristic equation that Chapter 5.4 solved by guessing e^(st).
L{df/dt} = sF(s) − f(0⁻)   ,   L{d²f/dt²} = s²F(s) − s f(0⁻) − f′(0⁻)
blocks.where: F(s) is the transform of f(t); f(0⁻) is the value just before the switch; f′(0⁻) is the value of its derivative just before the switch.

blocks.text: Two theorems give free checks at the two ends of the answer, so you never have to trust the algebra blindly.
f(0⁺) = lim(s→∞) sF(s)   ,   f(∞) = lim(s→0) sF(s)
blocks.where: the first is the initial value theorem; the second, the final value theorem, holds only when every pole of sF(s) has a negative real part, apart from at most one pole at s = 0. An undamped LC circuit has poles at ±jω, so its final value does not exist.

sections.h3: s-domain element models: memory becomes a source

blocks.text: A resistor has no memory: v = Ri holds at every instant, so V(s) = R I(s). The inductor and capacitor store energy, and their derivative relations pull the stored value into the transform as a source.

Inductor: v = L di/dt, so V(s) = sL I(s) − L i_L(0⁻). Model it as an impedance sL in series with a voltage source of value L i_L(0⁻), poled to push current the way the initial current was already flowing.

Capacitor: i = C dv/dt, so I(s) = sC V(s) − C v_C(0⁻), which rearranges to V(s) = (1/sC) I(s) + v_C(0⁻)/s. Model it as an impedance 1/sC in series with a source v_C(0⁻)/s. Note the 1/s: a stored 4 V becomes 4/s, because in the transformed picture that source must act for all time.

Parallel (Norton) versions swap the source for a current source: an inductor becomes sL in parallel with i_L(0⁻)/s, and a capacitor becomes 1/sC in parallel with C v_C(0⁻). Use whichever form keeps the node equations short. Now set s = jω and kill the initial-condition sources: every model becomes the impedance of Unit 3, Sinusoidal steady state.

sections.h3: Solve in s, then walk back to time

items: Freeze the circuit at t = 0⁻ and find i_L(0⁻) and v_C(0⁻).
Transform the sources: a DC source of A volts becomes A/s, A sin ωt becomes Aω/(s² + ω²), A cos ωt becomes As/(s² + ω²).
Replace R, L and C by the models above, initial-condition sources included.
Write KCL at each node (sum of V(s)/Z leaving the node = 0) or KVL round each mesh (sum of Z I(s) = source). It is plain algebra in s.
Solve for the wanted V(s) or I(s) as one rational function.
Split it into partial fractions and invert each term from the pair table.
Check with the initial and final value theorems, then against the answer from Chapter 5.3 or 5.4.

blocks.text: First check that the degree of the numerator is less than the degree of the denominator. If it is not, divide first, handle the polynomial part separately, and only then write the remainder as Σ K_i/(s − p_i). For distinct poles p₁, p₂, …, K_i = [(s − p_i)F(s)] evaluated at s = p_i, and each term inverts to K_i e^(p_i t). A pole repeated r times needs K/(s − p)^r terms, which invert to K t^(r−1) e^(pt)/(r−1)!; for r = 2 that is K t e^(pt), the t e^(−at) shape of critical damping.
The method never changes the physics. Same differential equation, same initial condition, same answer — the worked example below is the RC step of Chapter 5.3 done in s.

figure.caption: Top to bottom: the time-domain circuit becomes an s-domain circuit by transforming each element, is solved by ordinary algebra, and is inverted back to v(t) and i(t). The initial-condition sources and the partial-fraction step are where most marks are lost.

spec.aria: A downward chain from the time-domain circuit, through element transformation and an s-domain circuit, to an algebraic solution, partial fractions and the final time answer.
spec.title: Solving a transient in the s-domain

examples.question: A 10 V DC source is switched on at t = 0 into a series combination of R = 5 Ω and C = 0.1 F. Before switching, the capacitor already holds v_C(0⁻) = 4 V with the same polarity in which the source will charge it. Using the Laplace transform, find i(t) and v_C(t) for t ≥ 0, and check both ends.
steps: Initial state: v_C(0⁻) = 4 V and i(0⁻) = 0, since the source is not yet connected.
Transform the source: 10 V DC → 10/s. The capacitor becomes an impedance 1/(sC) = 1/(0.1s) = 10/s in series with a source v_C(0⁻)/s = 4/s.
KVL round the loop, with I(s) entering the capacitor terminal that was positive: 10/s = 5 I(s) + 10 I(s)/s + 4/s.
Inverse transform: i(t) = 1.2 e^(−2t) A. At t = 0⁺ this is 1.2 A, matching (10 − 4)/5, the current the 6 V difference drives through 5 Ω.
Inverse transform: v_C(t) = 10 − 6 e^(−2t) V. Check: v_C(0⁺) = 4 V, v_C(∞) = 10 V, and τ = RC = 0.5 s, so the decay rate is 1/τ = 2 s⁻¹.
examples.answer: i(t) = 1.2 e^(−2t) A and v_C(t) = 10 − 6 e^(−2t) V for t ≥ 0, with v_C(0⁺) = 4 V and v_C(∞) = 10 V.
examples.check:
R = 5.0
C = 0.1
Vs = 10.0
v0 = 4.0
tau = R * C
alpha = 1 / tau
i0 = (Vs - v0) / R
A = Vs - v0
print(i0)
print(alpha)
print(A)
print(Vs)
print(v0)

traps: Sign and scale of the initial-condition source. An inductor needs L i_L(0⁻) volts and a capacitor needs v_C(0⁻)/s volts in a series branch. Writing C v_C(0⁻) there is the parallel-form current source in the wrong place. The slip is silent and surfaces only at t = 0⁺.

Using f(0⁺) instead of f(0⁻) in the derivative rule. The theorem is stated with 0⁻ precisely because inductor current and capacitor voltage cannot jump; any other quantity can, and then the two values differ.

Applying the final value theorem to a circuit that never settles. If F(s) has a pole in the right half plane, or a pair on the jω axis as in an undamped LC, the limit does not exist and the 'steady state' you quote is fiction.
Dropping the 1/s or the ω. A constant A volts is A/s, not A, and A sin ωt is Aω/(s² + ω²), not A/(s² + ω²). A missing factor of ω is the commonest slip in the sinusoidal case.

quiz.q: State the derivative rule for L{df/dt} and say why the initial value is taken at 0⁻.
quiz.a: L{df/dt} = sF(s) − f(0⁻). The limit 0⁻ places the switching instant inside the integral, so a jump in f at t = 0 is captured; that is why the derivative rule carries the pre-switch value f(0⁻) as an ordinary number.

quiz.q: A capacitor is modelled as 1/sC in series with v_C(0⁻)/s. Why is the source divided by s?
quiz.a: Because it represents a constant voltage acting from t = 0 onwards, and the transform of a constant V is V/s. It is a source value, not a scaled impedance.

quiz.q: At t = 0 a 12 V DC source is applied to R = 4 Ω in series with L = 2 H, with i_L(0⁻) = 0. Find i(t) by the Laplace method.
The worked example gives V_C(s) = 10/s − 6/(s + 2). Use the initial and final value theorems to test it against v_C(0⁻) = 4 V and the expected steady state.
quiz.a: sV_C(s) = 10 − 6s/(s + 2). As s → ∞ this gives 10 − 6 = 4 V, matching v_C(0⁺). As s → 0 it gives 10 − 0 = 10 V, the DC steady state with the capacitor open. Both ends hold, so no term is missing.

quiz.q: What does a pole of I(s) at s = −2 tell you about i(t) without inverting?
quiz.a: It contributes a term K e^(−2t): a decaying exponential of time constant 1/2 = 0.5 s. A left-half-plane pole means the transient dies out, and its distance from the origin sets how fast.

beyond: Not for the exam. Every SPICE simulator stamps exactly these models into its matrix — sL and 1/sC are entries of modified nodal analysis — and inverts numerically instead of by partial fractions. Put s = jω and the same rational function becomes the frequency response plotted on a Bode plot. Control theory reads stability straight off the pole positions, which is where Chapter 5.8 leads. Search for 'residue' and 'rational function fitting' to see how a measured impedance becomes an s-domain model.
